summary: Quotes Leonardo of Pisa's Liber Abbaci (1202) heading and text naming the 'nine figures of the Indians'; Smith and Karpinski cite Boncompagni's 1857 edition. Shows Fibonacci himself labelled the system Indian.
limits: Does not show the route by which Leonardo learned them (he describes learning them in North Africa; not in this passage). 1911 work, partly superseded (it knew the Bakhshali manuscript only as 'probably' earlier than Gwalior; dates now debated). OCR text; quote checked against the OCR.

quote: the Arabs from the early ninth century on fully recognized the Hindu origin of the new numerals
summary: Concludes from Arabic writers on the Indian reckoning (al-Khwarizmi and others) that Islamic scholars from about 800 CE themselves called the system Hindu.

quote: derived from the use of the name Al-Khowarizmi in the opening sentence of the arithmetic, which reads, Dixit algoritmi
summary: Karpinski explains that 'algorism' came from the Latin arithmetic opening 'Dixit algoritmi' (the Algoritmi de numero Indorum), and that Robert of Chester translated al-Khwarizmi's algebra at Segovia in 1145 (Spanish Era 1183).
limits: Shows the Arabic-to-Latin step through named translators and a Latin text, but notes the author of the Latin arithmetic is unknown. 1915 scholarship; OCR text. Verifier: the quoted sentence gives no date; the 1145 Segovia date and the translation context come from elsewhere on the same scanned book.

title: Alberuni's India: an account of the religion, philosophy, literature, geography, chronology, astronomy, customs, laws and astrology of India about A.D. 1030
venue: Kegan Paul, Trench, Trubner, London (public-domain scan, Internet Archive)
ask_addressed: What is documented about the transmission of knowledge: Indian numerals and zero to the Islamic world to Europe (Fibonacci, al-Khwarizmi); Babylonian astronomy to Greece (Hipparchus); the Greek-to-Arabic-to-Latin translation movement; papermaking from China to the Islamic world to Europe; printing? Give dates, routes and the evidence.
quote: there came embassies from that part of India to Bagdad, and among them scholars, who brought along with them two books
summary: Al-Biruni (c. 1030) reports that under Caliph al-Mansur (753-774) Indian scholars brought the Brahmasiddhanta and Khandakhadyaka to Baghdad, where al-Fazari translated them; the Arabs thereby first learned a scientific astronomy.
limits: Written about 250 years after the event, and itself a retrospective claim; it concerns astronomical texts, not numerals as such. Translator's English of 1888/1910. Verifier: a literary report, not a dated document of the transfer; Gutas (separate candidate) doubts direct Sanskrit-to-Arabic translation, so directness is kept at documented only for the report itself.

Give dates, routes and the evidence.
quote: from about the middle of the eighth century to the end of the tenth, almost all non-literary and non-historical secular Greek books
summary: Gutas opens with the claim that nearly all secular Greek scientific and philosophical books available in the Byzantine East and Near East were translated into Arabic from about 750 to 1000, tying it to Abbasid state patronage.
limits: The quote is the first half of a sentence ('...were translated into Arabic'). The Arabic-to-Latin leg is not covered here. OCR text of the book, loaded from an Internet Archive copy.

title: Greek Thought, Arabic Culture: The Graeco-Arabic Translation Movement in Baghdad and Early 'Abbasid Society (2nd-4th/8th-10th c.)
ask_addressed: What is documented about the transmission of knowledge: Indian numerals and zero to the Islamic world to Europe (Fibonacci, al-Khwarizmi); Babylonian astronomy to Greece (Hipparchus); the Greek-to-Arabic-to-Latin translation movement; papermaking from China to the Islamic world to Europe; printing? Give dates, routes and the evidence.
quote: Indian scientific material in astronomy, astrology, mathematics, and medicine passed into Arabic mainly through Persian (Pahlavi) intermediaries during the 'Abbasid period
summary: Gutas argues that Indian science reached Arabic mainly via Pahlavi (Sasanian) intermediaries and that direct Sanskrit-to-Arabic translation is doubtful, qualifying a simple India-to-Baghdad story and stressing the Sasanian-Zoroastrian background of the translation movement.
limits: Quote normalised from OCR ('Pahlavj', 'inter- mediaries'). Sits against al-Biruni's report of direct work with Indian pandits; the two are not reconciled here. Gutas is a single (influential) scholarly position.

title: History of paper (Wikipedia)
ask_addressed: Which claims are disputed (date of the zero, 'Arabic numerals' naming, paper arrival, independent invention)?
quote: reported weavers, painters, goldsmiths, and silversmiths among the prisoners taken, but no papermakers
summary: Cites Bloom for the view that the story of Chinese prisoners from Talas (751) teaching papermaking at Samarkand is not reliable: no contemporary Arab source, the captive Du Huan lists no papermakers, and paper was in Central Asia earlier.
limits: Wikipedia pointer to Bloom, Paper Before Print (2001); Bloom's book was not opened (its Internet Archive copy is lending-only). The page also says paper reached Baghdad by 793 and Europe by 1085-1150 without primary text. Verifier: medium changed from 'trade' to 'unknown' (the page does not name a medium); the quoted sentence itself does not state an Islamic origin, which the page gives elsewhere ('probably' Islamic Iberian paper in the Missal of Silos), so directness stays inferred.
